title: What Is Lecithin and Why Is It Added to Chocolate and Other Foods?

seo.title: Lecithin: What It Is and Why Foods Use It
seo.meta_description: Lecithin is a phospholipid-rich mixture naturally present in foods such as egg yolk and soy. It is widely used as an emulsifier; in the EU it is E322.
seo.search_intent: Understand what lecithin is, where it comes from, and why it improves mixing, flow, and stability in chocolate and other foods.

excerpt: Lecithin is a phospholipid-rich mixture that can be obtained from sources including soy, sunflower, or egg. Its structure interacts with both water and fat, which makes it useful as an emulsifier. In the EU, lecithins are E322.
content_html:
Lecithin is a mixture of phospholipids used because it helps ingredients that tend to separate work together more effectively. EFSA notes that lecithins, E322 in the EU, also occur naturally in foods such as egg yolk, soybeans, peanuts, and corn. Commercial lecithin can come from several raw materials, including soy and sunflower.

Its usefulness comes from phospholipid structure: one region interacts well with water-like environments while another interacts with fat. That dual affinity supports emulsification and particle dispersion.

In chocolate, it helps control flow

Chocolate contains solid particles — cocoa, sugar, and sometimes milk solids — suspended in cocoa butter. A small amount of lecithin can reduce some friction among those particles and make chocolate flow more easily during refining, conching, pumping, and molding.

This allows manufacturers to tune viscosity without relying only on adding more cocoa butter. Lecithin does not define what chocolate is; it modifies how the fat phase and solid particles behave together.

It also helps foods where water and fat need to stay mixed

FDA lists soy lecithin among emulsifiers that help ingredients mix smoothly, prevent separation, and keep components dispersed. That is why it appears in margarine, baked goods, beverages, supplements, and many other formulations.

The exact job depends on the product. In one food it stabilizes an emulsion; in another it improves powder dispersibility, reduces sticking, or influences crystallization.

E322 does not identify a single source

The E number covers lecithins as an authorized additive category, but feedstock can vary. When source matters for allergen labeling, the product must follow applicable rules. Someone with an allergy should not assume all lecithin is sunflower-derived or, conversely, that all of it comes from soy.

Processing can reduce residual proteins, but specific allergen declarations and manufacturer information remain the practical references.

Lecithin is not the same as a large amount of added fat

Although lecithin is made of phospholipids, it is commonly used at small technological levels. Seeing it on a label does not mean it is one of the major fat sources in the product. Ingredient order and the nutrition facts provide the relevant context.

The practical rule: read lecithin or E322 as an emulsifier or dispersing ingredient. If source matters for allergy or preference, check the specific declaration; for nutrition, assess the entire food.

When interpreting this ingredient, separate technological function from nutritional quantity. An ingredient may be present at a small level to improve texture, mixing, or stability without representing a large share of the food by weight. Ingredient order and the nutrition panel provide context and keep a technical name from becoming a conclusion about the entire product.

faq.question: Where does lecithin come from?
faq.answer: Commercial sources can include soy, sunflower, and egg, while phospholipids occur naturally in many foods.

faq.question: Why is it used in chocolate?
faq.answer: It helps control viscosity, particle dispersion, and flow during processing.

faq.question: Does E322 always mean soy?
faq.answer: No. E322 identifies lecithins as an additive category; the source can vary.
